ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> Participants and data collection: Participants were recruited from a longitudinal study of survivors directly exposed to the October 7, 2023 attack at the Nova music festival in Israel (10).

> From an estimated population of 3,710 survivors (66% male; 76% aged 18-24 years), 1,268 were enrolled (772 men, 495 women, 1 unspecified; mean age=27.17 years, SD=6.75).

> All participants provided informed consent.

> Whether participants had attended a party since October 7 and whether they had experienced an additional traumatic event since October 7 (yes/no) were compared between latent classes.

> Re-fitting our LCA onto the TP3 drug indicators (303 participants with TP3 drug-use data, 302 of whom were also classified at TP2; the remaining participant had only a partial TP2 response), we again identified two classes: the same Low-load/High-load structure identified at TP2 (Figure 3B-C), suggesting that this was a stable feature of the sample.

> High-load participants were more likely than Low-load participants to have attended a party since October 7.

> Our findings do not tell a simple story of either benefit or harm from ongoing drug use: there is no clear evidence that drug use in our participants exacerbated their PTSD symptoms, but also no clear evidence that drug use resolved them.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Objective: Drug use after trauma is common, but polydrug use patterns, motives, and associations with subsequent symptoms are poorly understood.
We examined these associations among mass-casualty terror attack survivors, 72% of whom used drugs immediately before trauma exposure.

Methods: Survivors of the October 7, 2023 Nova Festival attack reported use of six drug types (alcohol, cannabis, ketamine, stimulants, MDMA, psychedelics) and motives (avoidance, emotional regulation, self-medication, sleep, recreation) longitudinally at three timepoints (TP): 1-6 months (N=772), 8-12 months (N=453), and 17-24 months (N=302) post-attack.
Separate latent class analyses of TP2 data characterized drug use, motives, and their combination.
Linear regression and mixed-effects models examined associations between class membership and PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5) scores, adjusting for age, sex, time since trauma, and TP1 PCL-5 scores.
Results: At TP2, 70% reported polydrug use, 17% used one drug, and 13% reported no use.

The high drug-load class (mean 4.6 drug types) had lower PCL-5 scores than the low drug-load class (mean 1.5 drug types); this difference was evident among participants using ≥4 drug types and persisted through TP3.
The self-medication-motive class had higher PCL-5 scores than the recreational-motive class.
In joint analyses, recreational-motive users at both low and high drug loads had lower PCL-5 scores than participants reporting self-medication motives and primarily cannabis use.
Conclusions: Polydrug use was common among the mass-trauma survivors in our study.
Selfmedication motives were associated with higher PTSD symptom severity than recreational motives.
Unexpectedly, higher polydrug use was associated with lower PTSD symptom scores.
Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is associated with the use of potentially addictive drugs; causes of the association may include self-medication for PTSD symptoms (1, 2).

Research on PTSD and SUDs has usually focused on drugs other than the psychedelics and entactogens that have moved toward clinical use for treatment or prevention of PTSD (5) (6) (7).

text.text: However, outside supervised treatment protocols, trauma survivors already use these drugs on their own, at uncontrolled doses, with other drugs, and in settings unlike those of clinical trials.
These naturalistic patterns of drug use have rarely been examined together with motives for use in the context of emergent PTSD symptoms after trauma exposure.
A rare opportunity to address this arose in the aftermath of the October 7, 2023 attack at the Nova music festival in Israel.

Several thousand festival attendees were directly exposed to a mass-casualty terror attack on a single day, creating a large and identifiable survivor population that we have followed prospectively with repeated assessments of drug use (though not SUD symptoms), motives for use, and posttraumatic symptoms for two years since the event (10) (11) (12).

text.text: We previously found in this sample that attendees who had taken MDMA shortly before the attack, thereby experiencing the attack under the influence of MDMA, had more favorable posttraumatic outcomes than those who had not used any drugs that day.

Their outcomes over the first four months after the attack included lower psychological distress, greater social interaction, and better sleep, accompanied by a perception that the drug use had been helpful during the event (11).

text.text: In contrast, cannabis and/or alcohol use shortly before the attack was associated with greater PTSD symptoms, psychological distress and poorer sleep, compared to use of no drugs (11).

text.text: In the current report we characterize motives for, and patterns of, ongoing drug use among Nova festival survivors assessed longitudinally 8 to 24 months after the attack.
Using latent class analysis (LCA), we identify classes based on (a) types of drugs used, (b) motives for drug use, and (c) their combination.
We then examine class differences in severity of emergent PTSD symptoms.
Based on prior work(e.g. 3), we expected self-medication motives to be associated with higher PTSD symptom severity.
Participants and data collection: Participants were recruited from a longitudinal study of survivors directly exposed to the October 7, 2023 attack at the Nova music festival in Israel (10).
text.formatted: Participants and data collection: Participants were recruited from a longitudinal study of survivors directly exposed to the October 7, 2023 attack at the Nova music festival in Israel <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(10)</ref>.

text.text: From an estimated population of 3,710 survivors (66% male; 76% aged 18-24 years), 1,268 were enrolled (772 men, 495 women, 1 unspecified; mean age=27.17 years, SD=6.75).
Recruitment was conducted collaboratively with Safeheart (a nonprofit organization supporting Nova survivors), support groups on social media, and word of mouth.
Data were collected between November 2, 2023 and September 26, 2025.
All participants provided informed consent.
The study was approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee of the University of Haifa (Approval No.
Assessments were performed longitudinally at three post-event timepoints (TPs): TP1 (1-6 months), TP2 (8-12 months), and TP3 (17-24 months) (Figure 1A).

text.text: The main analyses here included participants aged ≥18 years who completed both TP1 and TP2 assessments.
Longitudinal analyses were restricted to participants with data available at TP3.

text.text: Measures: Types of drug use were reported at TP1 for the traumatic event and at each follow-up assessment (TP2 and TP3), with a time frame of the past 30 days, via a multiple-choice questionnaire with an optional free-text field.
For each drug used, participants also reported how many times they had used it in the past 30 days; these frequencies were used only to describe the latent classes (Supplementary Methods).
Reported drugs were collapsed into six categories: alcohol, cannabis, ketamine, stimulants, MDMA, and psychedelics (Supplementary Methods).
Binary indicators of use/nonuse were assigned to summarize patterns of co-use and derive latent classes.
Motives for drug use were reported using a checklist with optional free-text responses.
After collapsing sparse categories, we retained five motive categories: avoidance, emotional regulation, self-medication ("to cure myself"), sleep, and recreational use.
PTSD symptom severity was assessed at TP1, TP2, and TP3 using the PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5) (10).
text.formatted: PTSD symptom severity was assessed at TP1, TP2, and TP3 using the PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5) <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(10)</ref>.

text.text: Total scores were treated as a continuous variable for most analyses; we also used the established clinical cutoff (≥33) for specific subgroup analyses.
Demographic variables used as covariates were age at recruitment and sex.
Time elapsed between October 7 and each outcome assessment was also included as a covariate.
Whether participants had attended a party since October 7 and whether they had experienced an additional traumatic event since October 7 (yes/no) were compared between latent classes.
Patterns of drug co-use, and motives, were visualized using UpSet plots.
LCAs classified participants in three ways: (a) types of drugs used, (b) drug-use motives, and (c) a combined model incorporating both domains.
Details of model selection and robustness analyses are in the Supplementary Methods.
Because the drug-use classes were derived empirically, analyses of drug load and specific drug combinations were exploratory.
We then used multiple linear regression to examine associations between latent class membership (for each of three types of classification) and severity of PTSD symptoms.
In additional analyses, we examined the total number of drugs used (0-6) as a categorical predictor.
These regressions were repeated in subgroups above or below the cutoff for probable PTSD (PCL-5 ≥33).
Associations of latent class membership with party attendance and additional traumaticevent exposure were evaluated with Pearson's chi-squares.

Longitudinal changes in PCL-5 scores between TP2 and TP3 were examined using linear mixed-effects models with all available PCL-5 observations, including fixed effects for timepoint, TP2 latent class, and their interaction, with participant-specific random intercepts.
Regression models were adjusted for age, sex, and time elapsed since October 7.
Primary analyses were additionally adjusted for baseline PTSD symptom severity (TP1 PCL-5 score).
Mixed-effects models were adjusted for age and sex.
Statistical analyses were conducted using R software.

text.text: Only 59 of 453 participants (13%) reported no drug use that month.
The most common patterns were alcohol and cannabis (n=79) and cannabis only (n=37); other patterns involved combinations of three or more drugs, typically including psychedelics and MDMA.

Collapsing the polydrug combinations into a single drug while ignoring others indicated that people using MDMA or psychedelics (along with other drugs) showed lowest levels of PTSD symptoms: after adjustment, MDMA-users scored 4.28 points lower than non-MDMA-users (β=-4.28, Bonferroni-corrected p=.026) and psychedelic-users scored 3.90 points lower than nonpsychedelic-users (β=-3.90, corrected p=.031).
In contrast, the differences for alcohol, cannabis, ketamine, and stimulants were not significantly different from non-users of these drugs (Supplementary Figure S1).

This yielded a three-class solution (Figure 2E), labelled 1) "Self-medication and high cannabis use" (Self Med High Can; n=190); 2) "Recreation / emotional management and high polydrug use" (Rec Emo High Poly; n=122); and 3) "Recreation and low drug use" (Rec Low Use; n=79).

text.text: In previously reported results from this sample of mass-trauma survivors, we found that being acutely under the influence of MDMA or psychedelics during the event was perceived as helpful for trauma processing.
For MDMA, this was accompanied by lower mental distress, better sleep, and more social interactions in the four months after the event (11).

text.text: Here, we report follow-up data on ongoing drug use and its relationship to PCL-5 scores up to two years after that traumatic event.
We report three main findings.

First, at TP2 (8-12 months), ongoing polydrug use was common, and use of more drug types (including, though not limited to, MDMA and psychedelics) was unexpectedly associated with lower PCL-5 scores compared with use of fewer drug types (mostly, but not only, alcohol and cannabis).

Additionally, the association between higher polydrug use and lower PTSD symptom severity persisted after adjustment for baseline (TP1) PTSD symptoms, and among participants whose PCL-5 scores exceeded the cutoff for PTSD.

Second, motives for drug use were associated with PTSD symptom severity regardless of the number of drug types used: participants reporting self-medication motives had higher PCL-5 scores than those reporting recreational motives.

Third, the association between lower PCL-5 scores and the use of more drug types was largely preserved longitudinally at TP3 (17-24 months), although PTSD symptom severity increased modestly over time regardless of the number of drug types used.
Increased drug use after mass trauma is well documented.
Several studies reported increased drug use among Manhattan residents after the World Trade Center attack (13, 14) , and meta-analyses show increases after other terrorist attacks (15, 16).

text.text: Two surveys of Israeli adults conducted about one month after October 7, 2023 found comparable increases.

In one, 34% reported increased use of at least one drug, most often tobacco, sedatives, pain medication, and alcohol (only 5.5% reported increased cannabis use), and greater trauma exposure predicted increased use of sedatives but not other drugs (17).

text.text: In the other study, 19% reported increased drug use, most often alcohol, followed by sedatives and cannabis; increased use was more likely after direct exposure (OR=5.75) and with greater psychological distress (OR=1.80) (18).

text.text: Increased drug use after trauma is often viewed as a maladaptive coping strategy, a form of "self-medication" in which people use drugs that temporarily reduce specific posttraumatic symptoms (18) (19) (20).

text.text: The effect of such self-medication remains unclear.
In a large epidemiological study, self-medication of PTSD symptoms was associated with greater psychiatric comorbidity and more suicide attempts (3).
Although causality is difficult to establish, drug use after trauma is generally considered detrimental to clinical outcomes (20, 21).

text.text: Unexpectedly, our data do not support this association.

In fact, Nova survivors who used more drug types had lower PTSD symptom severity than those who used fewer, and this association persisted after adjustment for baseline symptoms and over the second year after the attack.
Several differences between our study and previous work may explain this discrepancy.

First, prior research has largely examined the relationship between PTSD and SUDs, typically in clinical, help-seeking, or veteran cohorts in which problematic drug use was the defining feature (20, (22) (23) (24) (25).
text.formatted: First, prior research has largely examined the relationship between PTSD and SUDs, typically in clinical, help-seeking, or veteran cohorts in which problematic drug use was the defining feature <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(22)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(23)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(24)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(25)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, our cohort comprised civilian survivors of a mass terror attack at a music festival, most of whom had a history of recreational drug use before the attack and many of whom developed clinically significant PTSD symptoms after it.

Increased drug use after trauma does not necessarily indicate disorder: in a meta-analysis of adults exposed to terrorist attacks, 6% increased their alcohol consumption, but the prevalence of alcohol use disorder was no higher than in the general population (16).
text.formatted: Increased drug use after trauma does not necessarily indicate disorder: in a meta-analysis of adults exposed to terrorist attacks, 6% increased their alcohol consumption, but the prevalence of alcohol use disorder was no higher than in the general population <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(16)</ref>.

text.text: Second, prior work has focused mainly on alcohol, cannabis, sedatives, and opioids (17, 18), and has often examined a single drug in isolation (e.g. 21, 26, 27).
text.formatted: Second, prior work has focused mainly on alcohol, cannabis, sedatives, and opioids <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(17,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18)</ref>, and has often examined a single drug in isolation (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">26,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">27)</ref>.

text.text: We characterized naturalistic polydrug use patterns, which were complex and varied across individuals.
Our "high load" class was distinguished by use of MDMA, psychedelics, and ketamine, drug types under clinical investigation as medications for PTSD (6, 8).
text.formatted: Our "high load" class was distinguished by use of MDMA, psychedelics, and ketamine, drug types under clinical investigation as medications for PTSD <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8)</ref>.

text.text: In single-drug analyses, users of MDMA and psychedelics showed the largest symptom differences relative to non-users.
However, because these drugs were almost always used as part of a complex polydrug pattern, the association cannot be attributed to any single drug or drug class.
Motives for use appear to matter: drug load and selfmedication motives were associated with symptom severity in opposite directions.
Our observational study has several limitations.
First, we did not assess prior or emergent symptoms of SUDs, nor perceptions of benefit from ongoing drug use.
Thus, we cannot draw direct conclusions about the benefits or harms of the ongoing drug use reported.
Second, class differences in PCL-5 scores, even when statistically significant, were small in absolute terms.

The sample as a whole had exceedingly high PCL-5 scores, reflecting severe persisting PTSD symptoms, more than has been seen in other longitudinal studies of trauma survivors, including mass-trauma survivors (28, 29).
text.formatted: The sample as a whole had exceedingly high PCL-5 scores, reflecting severe persisting PTSD symptoms, more than has been seen in other longitudinal studies of trauma survivors, including mass-trauma survivors <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(28,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">29)</ref>.

text.text: Third, drug load may partly reflect social re-engagement rather than successful selftreatment.
High-load participants were more likely than Low-load participants to have attended a party since October 7.
For festival survivors, returning to parties and their associated drug use may mark a return to pre-trauma routines, which may be more accessible to those with fewer symptoms.

Our findings do not tell a simple story of either benefit or harm from ongoing drug use: there is no clear evidence that drug use in our participants exacerbated their PTSD symptoms, but also no clear evidence that drug use resolved them.

We cannot answer the central counterfactual question: how many participants' PCL-5 scores would now be either lower or higher if they had not used their self-selected combinations of drugs at self-selected frequencies?
The current data might reflect a combination of desirable and undesirable outcomes for each pattern of drug use and each class of motives.
Polydrug use was common among Nova festival survivors up to two years after the attack.

Higher drug load, involving more frequent use of MDMA and psychedelics, was associated with lower PTSD symptom severity, whereas self-medication motives, accompanied by near-daily cannabis use, were associated with higher severity.
The cannabis finding is consistent with our earlier report that cannabis use during the attack predicted worse psychological outcomes (11), and with prospective data from US veterans (21, 30).
text.formatted: The cannabis finding is consistent with our earlier report that cannabis use during the attack predicted worse psychological outcomes (11), and with prospective data from US veterans <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(21,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">30)</ref>.

text.text: This, together with the well-documented risks of alcohol in PTSD (20, 22), suggest that clinicians should ask trauma survivors not only which drugs they use but why.
text.formatted: This, together with the well-documented risks of alcohol in PTSD <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22)</ref>, suggest that clinicians should ask trauma survivors not only which drugs they use but why.

text.text: Finally, non-addictive drug use has been proposed to be instrumental, serving goals such as improved social interaction or coping with stress (31).
text.formatted: Finally, non-addictive drug use has been proposed to be instrumental, serving goals such as improved social interaction or coping with stress <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(31)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings fit this framework: motives for use, not only amount or type of drug, were associated with posttraumatic symptoms.
The MDMA and psychedelic findings are compatible with, but do not demonstrate, a therapeutic effect, and do not support unsupervised use as treatment.

Although long-term use of addictive drugs can be harmful, recreational use of some drug classes, such as MDMA and psychedelics, may be associated with better outcomes in some people under some circumstances, including after severe trauma.
